title: How to use the preview pane in Finder on Mac: show, resize, and fix it
metaTitle: How to Use the Preview Pane in Finder on Mac
description: Learn how to use the preview pane in Finder on Mac. Turn it on with View > Show Preview, resize it, and fix missing thumbnails fast.
targetKeyword: how to use the preview pane in finder on mac
intro: To use the preview pane in Finder on Mac, open a Finder window, select a file, and choose View > Show Preview. The pane then shows that file on the right side of the window, and you can drag its divider to resize it or choose View > Hide Preview to close it.
tldr: Open a Finder window, select a file, and choose View > Show Preview.
Column view shows the pane by default. Icon and List views need you to turn it on.
Tick Show Quick Actions in View > Show Preview Options to rotate images or make PDFs from the pane.
Apple's pages list no keyboard shortcut for the pane. MacMost lists ⇧⌘P, so test it before you rely on it.

blocks.text: The preview pane is the strip on the right side of a Finder window. Select a file or folder, and the pane shows a preview of it. You can check a photo, skim a PDF, or confirm you have the right spreadsheet without opening it in another app. That matters most when a folder holds many files with similar names. Apple calls this feature the Preview pane in its Mac help, so this guide uses the same name.
Turn on the preview pane in Finder

Open any Finder window and click a file once so it is highlighted. Then choose View > Show Preview from the menu bar at the top of the screen. The pane appears on the right side of the window and shows the file you selected. If you do not see it, check that menu first. Icon and List views keep the pane off until you turn it on.

Apple's help page for the pane uses the same path. It says to select a folder or file, and if you do not see the pane, to choose View > Show Preview. If the pane still does not appear, the view you are in is the usual cause. The next section covers that.
Which Finder views show the preview pane

The pane behaves differently in each view. Column view shows it by default, so many people first meet the pane there. Icon and List views need you to switch it on by hand. Once you know this, you can pick the view that suits the task and turn the pane on only when you need it.

items: Column view: the pane shows by default. Select a file to see its preview on the right.
Icon view: choose View > Show Preview to turn the pane on.
List view: choose View > Show Preview to turn the pane on.

blocks.text: Column view is handy when you move through nested folders, because each level sits in its own column. Icon view suits a grid of thumbnails. List view suits sorting by name, date, or size. Pick the view first, then decide whether the pane earns its space.

If you use the sidebar a lot, read [how to change the sidebar in Finder](/how-to/change-the-sidebar-in-finder). The sidebar and the pane work well together. Set the sidebar once, then use the pane to check what is inside each folder.
Choose which details the pane shows

The pane is not a fixed box of information. Apple says the options depend on the file type, so an image shows different choices from a text file. Open View > Show Preview Options and tick the boxes for the details you want. Untick anything you never read, so the pane stays short.

Try this once with a typical file. Click the file, look at the pane, then untick what you do not need. Next, click a file of another type, such as a PDF or a video, and see what changes. That quick check saves guessing later, when the pane is the only thing you have time to read.

rows: Turns the pane on or off in the current window
Lists per-file-type checkboxes for the details you want
Lets the pane run tasks such as rotating an image or creating a PDF
Brings back file thumbnails when they go missing
blocks.caption: The four settings that matter most for the pane, per Apple and MacRumors.

blocks.text: Resize the preview pane or close it

Look for the thin divider line between the file list and the pane. Drag it left to make the pane wider. That helps with long text or large images. Drag it right to give the file list more room. Apple describes the same divider on its help page.

To close the pane, drag the divider all the way to the right. You can also choose View > Hide Preview. Both work. The menu is quicker when you switch the pane on and off often. The drag is quicker when you only want a little more room.
Use Quick Actions from the pane

Quick Actions sit at the bottom of the pane once you choose View > Show Preview and tick Show Quick Actions in the Preview Options list. Apple uses rotating an image and creating a PDF as examples. To change which actions appear, click More and choose Customize. That opens Extensions settings, where you can review the list.
Preview pane or Quick Look: which one to use

Finder has a second way to look at a file. Select it and press Space to open Quick Look, which shows a larger preview in its own window. The pane stays inside the Finder window and updates as you move through the folder. Use the pane to scan many files one after another. Use Quick Look when one file needs a closer look.
Worked example: check photos before you share them

Say you have a folder called Trip with several photos, and you need to send only a few of them. Choose View > Show Preview, then click each photo in turn. The pane shows each one large enough to judge focus and framing. You can spot a blurry shot or closed eyes in seconds, without opening each image in another app.

If one photo is sideways, select it and use the rotate action at the bottom of the pane. That works only with Show Quick Actions ticked, because Apple says that checkbox must be selected for tasks such as rotating an image. When you have picked your photos, select them together and drag them into your email or message as usual.
A quick routine for a messy Downloads folder

A Downloads folder often holds receipts, scans, and screenshots with names like IMG or Scan. Turn on the pane, then press the down arrow to move through the list. The pane follows each file as you move, so you can read the receipt, skip the screenshot, and keep going.

Untick the details you never need before you start, so each preview stays easy to scan. When you find the file you want, double-click it to open it in its normal app. The pane is for deciding. Double-clicking is for opening.
Why the preview pane is missing

Most missing panes come down to three causes: the view, the menu setting, or the file. First check that the window is in Column view, or that you turned the pane on in Icon or List view. Next check View > Show Preview, because the setting may have been switched off by accident. Last, try a file that Finder can preview, such as a photo.

A simple reset helps when the pane seems stuck. Choose View > Hide Preview, then choose View > Show Preview again. This does not change or move any of your files, so you can try it first, before any deeper fix.
Fix missing thumbnails in Finder

Thumbnails are the small pictures Finder draws for each file. When they stop showing, the preview can look broken even when the pane is on. MacRumors describes a fix for missing file icon previews in macOS Finder. It has four steps, and you do them in order.

items: Choose View > Show View Options and tick Show Preview Icon.
Search for ThumbnailsAgent, select com.apple.quicklook.ThumbnailsAgent, and restart it.
Relaunch Finder. Hold Option, right-click the Finder icon in the Dock, and choose Relaunch.

blocks.text: Give Finder a few seconds, then open a folder of images in Icon view. If the thumbnails return, you are done. If they still do not appear, restart the Mac and check again.

blocks.title: Before you touch settings files
blocks.text: Some community threads suggest deleting com.apple.finder.plist when view settings will not stick. That file holds your Finder preferences, so deleting it resets them. Copy it somewhere safe first, for example to your Desktop, and only then remove the original.
Mistakes people make with the preview pane

items: Mixing up the pane with the Preview app. The pane lives inside Finder. The Preview app is a separate program for opening and editing files.
Looking for the pane in Icon or List view before turning it on. Those views keep it off until you choose View > Show Preview.
Expecting every file to preview. Apple's iCloud help says a file without a thumbnail cannot be previewed there, so test with a photo or PDF first.
Trusting a shortcut from a blog without testing it. Apple's keyboard shortcut page lists none for the pane.
Deleting settings files without a backup. Copy the file before any reset, so you can put it back.

blocks.text: Is there a shortcut for the preview pane?

Many people look for a key combination before they look at the menu. MacMost says ⇧⌘P, which is Shift-Command-P, toggles the pane on and off. Apple's keyboard shortcut page does not list a shortcut for the Preview pane or for Show Preview Options. So treat the shortcut as a third-party claim until you test it.

Test it yourself. Open a Finder window, select a file, and press ⇧⌘P. If the pane appears or closes, the shortcut works on your Mac. If nothing changes, use View > Show Preview instead. The menu path is the one Apple documents, so it is the safe fallback.
Previewing files on iCloud.com instead

The pane is part of Finder on your Mac. iCloud.com has no equivalent pane. Apple's iCloud help says to select a file, click More in the top-right corner, and choose Preview. Pressing the Space bar with the file selected also previews it. Double-clicking opens the file in a new tab, which is a different action.

If you work across a Mac and the web, expect the steps to differ. Keep the Finder steps for your Mac, and use the iCloud steps only in a browser. Mixing them up is the fastest way to waste a few minutes.
Which macOS version these steps cover

Apple's help pages show macOS 27 Golden Gate as the current release. The preview pane steps on those pages are not tied to one version. The menu wording was not checked against macOS 26 Tahoe or earlier. If your View menu looks different, look for the same items by name, such as Show Preview and Show Preview Options.
Next steps once the pane works

Once the pane works, a few related settings help it fit your work. If you need to see where a file lives while you preview it, read [how to show the path bar in Finder](/how-to/show-the-path-bar-in-finder). If you need hidden files, read [how to show hidden files in Finder](/how-to/show-hidden-files-in-finder).

Set the details once in Show Preview Options, and you will rarely need that menu again. Keep Quick Actions on if you rotate or convert files often. Turn the pane off when you only need the file list, because the list gets the full window back.

faq.question: Where is the Preview pane in Finder on Mac?
faq.answer: It sits on the right side of a Finder window. Turn it on with View > Show Preview. Column view shows it by default, while Icon and List views need you to switch it on.

faq.question: Is there a keyboard shortcut for the Preview pane?
faq.answer: MacMost lists ⇧⌘P, but Apple's keyboard shortcut page does not list one for the pane. Test the shortcut on your Mac, and use View > Show Preview if it does nothing.

faq.question: How do I get the Preview pane in Icon view?
faq.answer: Choose View > Show Preview while the Icon view window is active. Icon and List views keep the pane off until you turn it on.

faq.question: Why are my Finder thumbnails not showing?
faq.answer: Choose View > Show View Options and tick Show Preview Icon. Then restart com.apple.quicklook.ThumbnailsAgent in Activity Monitor and relaunch Finder.

faq.question: Can I preview files on iCloud.com?
faq.answer: Yes, but iCloud.com has no Preview pane. Select the file, click More in the top-right corner, and choose Preview. Pressing Space with the file selected also works.

faq.question: Is the Preview pane the same as the Preview app?
faq.answer: No. The pane sits inside a Finder window and shows the selected item. The Preview app is a separate program for opening and editing files.

faq.question: Which macOS version do these steps cover?
faq.answer: Apple's help pages show macOS 27 Golden Gate as the current release. The menu wording was not checked on macOS 26 Tahoe or earlier, so compare the names on your own View menu.

appliesTo: Finder on macOS 27 Golden Gate, per Apple's current help page
requirements: A Mac running macOS 27 Golden Gate or a recent macOS release
A Finder window open to a folder with at least one file in it
A file that has a preview, such as a photo or a PDF

steps.name: Open a Finder window
steps.text: Click the Finder icon in the Dock. A Finder window opens. Browse to the folder that holds the file you want to check.
steps.tip: If a Finder window is already open, skip this step and use that window.

steps.name: Pick Column view for the quickest start
steps.text: Choose View > as Columns. Column view shows the Preview pane by default, so you see it without another setting. You can switch to Icon or List view later.
steps.tip: In Icon or List view, you must turn on the pane yourself in the Show Preview step.

steps.name: Select the file or folder
steps.text: Click the file once so it is highlighted. The pane shows the item you select, so click the file you care about.
steps.tip: Clicking another file updates the pane to match it.

steps.name: Turn on the Preview pane
steps.text: Choose View > Show Preview. The pane appears on the right side of the window and shows the selected file. Use this step in Icon or List view, where the pane is off by default.
steps.tip: MacMost lists ⇧⌘P for this. Apple does not list it, so test it, and use the menu if nothing happens.

steps.name: Read the preview and details
steps.text: Look at the pane for the preview and any details you turned on. Select another file, and the pane updates to show it. Practice with a few file types so you know what each one looks like.
steps.tip: Try an image, a PDF, and a plain text file.

steps.name: Choose the details to show
steps.text: Choose View > Show Preview Options. Tick the boxes for the details you want. The list depends on file type, so an image and a text file show different choices.
steps.tip: Untick anything you never read so the pane stays easy to scan.

steps.name: Turn on Quick Actions
steps.text: In the Show Preview Options list, make sure Show Quick Actions is ticked. Quick Actions such as rotating an image or creating a PDF then appear at the bottom of the pane.
steps.tip: If you do not see Quick Actions, check that the pane itself is on.

steps.name: Resize the pane
steps.text: Drag the thin divider line between the file list and the pane. Drag left to make the pane wider. Drag right to give the file list more room.
steps.tip: Dragging the divider all the way to the right closes the pane.

steps.name: Hide the pane when you are done
steps.text: Choose View > Hide Preview to turn the pane off. The file list then gets the full width of the window.
steps.tip: Choose View > Show Preview again whenever you want the pane back.

shortcuts.action: Toggle the Preview pane (unverified, test first)

troubleshooting.problem: The pane is missing in Icon or List view
troubleshooting.fix: Choose View > Show Preview. Those views keep the pane off until you turn it on. Column view shows it by default.

troubleshooting.problem: The pane is blank for some files
troubleshooting.fix: Some files have no thumbnail, and Apple's iCloud help says those cannot be previewed. Select a photo or PDF to confirm the pane works, then return to the file type that failed.

troubleshooting.problem: Thumbnails do not show in Icon view
troubleshooting.fix: Choose View > Show View Options and tick Show Preview Icon. Then restart com.apple.quicklook.ThumbnailsAgent in Activity Monitor and relaunch Finder.

troubleshooting.problem: Quick Actions are missing from the pane
troubleshooting.fix: Choose View > Show Preview Options and tick Show Quick Actions. The pane must also be on, so check View > Show Preview first.

troubleshooting.problem: View settings do not stick after a restart
troubleshooting.fix: Copy com.apple.finder.plist from your Library > Preferences folder before any reset. Community posts suggest deleting it, which resets Finder preferences. Try this only as a last resort, with a backup in place.

troubleshooting.problem: You are looking for the pane on iCloud.com
troubleshooting.fix: iCloud.com has no Preview pane. Select the file, click More in the top-right corner, and choose Preview, or press Space.
